name: 2-minute start
steps: Set a 2-minute timer and touch {task} until it rings. Stopping right after is completely allowed.
If you'd like, go another 2 minutes. Or stop here and call it a win.
literal_version: Press 'Start the 2-minute timer' below. Work on {task} until the timer ends. You may stop when it ends.
Optional: start another 2-minute timer and continue {task}.
phrasings: Just two minutes with {task}, then you get to decide if you keep going.
Tiny deal: two minutes on {task}. That's all this asks.
why_it_works: Promising only two minutes makes the starting wall much lower, and once you're moving, carrying on usually costs less than starting.

name: Ugly first draft
steps: Write the messiest possible first sentence for {task}. Bad on purpose counts.
Add one more messy sentence. Fixing is for later-you.
literal_version: Type one sentence about {task}. Spelling and quality do not matter.
Type one more sentence. Do not edit the first one.
phrasings: What if the first line of {task} was allowed to be terrible?
Let's make a gloriously ugly first sentence for {task}.
why_it_works: Perfectionism often hides inside task paralysis; giving yourself permission to write badly removes the pressure that keeps the page blank.

name: Body doubling
steps: Turn on body-double mode. I'll sit right here with you while you look at {task}.
Keep me open beside you. Do the next tiny piece of {task} while I keep you company.
literal_version: Press 'Start body-double mode' below. A calm timer will run beside you. Then open {task}.
Keep the timer running. Do one small part of {task}.
phrasings: Want some company? I can stay with you while you open {task}.
How about we do {task} side by side for a bit?
why_it_works: Having a calm presence nearby lowers the activation energy to start; many ADHD folks find working 'with someone' much easier than working alone.

name: Interest hook
steps: Skim {task} and find the one bit that's even slightly interesting. Start there, not at the beginning.
Stay with that interesting bit for one more small piece.
literal_version: Look over {task}. Choose the part that interests you most. Start with that part.
Do one more small piece of that same part.
phrasings: Which part of {task} is the least boring? Let's sneak in through that door.
Curiosity can be a side entrance. What's one interesting corner of {task}?
why_it_works: Interest is a strong fuel for ADHD brains; entering through the interesting part borrows that energy for the rest.

name: Race the timer
steps: Quick game: set 90 seconds and see how many words (or lines) of {task} you can get down before it ends.
Want a rematch? Try to beat your last count.
literal_version: Start a 90-second timer. Write as many words for {task} as you can before it ends. Count them.
Optional: start another 90-second timer and try to write more words than last time.
phrasings: Want to turn {task} into a tiny game?
Ninety-second sprint on {task}, just for fun?
why_it_works: A tiny game adds urgency and novelty, two things that help an interest-based nervous system get moving.

name: When-then plan
steps: Finish this sentence out loud: "When I ___, I'll open {task}." Pick something that happens soon, like finishing your water.
When that moment comes, just open {task}. That's the whole plan.
literal_version: Say this sentence and fill the blank: 'When I ___, I will open {task}.' Choose an action you will do in the next 10 minutes.
When you finish that action, open {task}.
phrasings: Let's hook {task} onto something you're already going to do.
Want to pick a 'when' for {task} instead of a 'now'?
why_it_works: If-then plans hand the decision to a cue in your environment, so starting needs less willpower in the moment.

name: Change location
steps: Take your laptop (or notes) somewhere different — another chair, the library, the kitchen table — then open {task} there.
Settle in. First move in the new spot: look at {task} for one minute.
literal_version: Pick up your laptop. Move to a different seat or room. Then open {task}.
In the new place, look at {task} for one minute.
phrasings: Sometimes a new spot makes a new start. Want to move somewhere for {task}?
Change of scenery for {task}?
why_it_works: A new place breaks the loop of cues tied to scrolling and stuck feelings, and the small novelty helps attention switch on.

name: Turn it into a question
steps: Turn {task} into one question you're curious about, like "What is this really asking me?" Write the question down.
Write the first half-answer that comes to mind. Rough is perfect.
literal_version: Write one question about {task}. Example: 'What is this assignment asking me to do?'
Write a short answer to your question. It can be incomplete.
phrasings: What if {task} was a question instead of a chore?
Let's get curious: what's {task} actually asking?
why_it_works: Questions invite curiosity instead of pressure, and curiosity is easier to start from than obligation.

name: One-song start
steps: Put on one song you like. Work on {task} only until the song ends.
Another song? Same deal — stop whenever the music does.
literal_version: Play one song. Work on {task} until the song ends. Then you may stop.
Optional: play one more song and continue {task}.
phrasings: One song, one tiny bit of {task}?
Let a song be your timer for {task}.
why_it_works: Music gives time a shape you can feel, and a familiar song can act as a start signal for your brain.

name: Just open it
steps: Just open {task}. That's the whole step. Looking at it is optional.
Now that it's open, scroll to wherever you left off. Nothing more.
literal_version: Open {task}. You do not need to do anything else.
Scroll to the place where you stopped last time.
phrasings: Smallest possible step: just open {task}.
What if you only opened {task} and called that a win?
why_it_works: Opening the thing is often the hardest part; making it the entire goal turns an impossible wall into one click.

name: Transition ritual
steps: Mini ritual: close one tab you don't need, take three slow breaths, then look at {task}.
Keep the calm going. Read the first line of {task}.
literal_version: Close one tab you are not using. Breathe in and out slowly three times. Then look at {task}.
Read the first line of {task}.
phrasings: Let's give your brain a little doorway into {task}.
A tiny reset before {task}?
why_it_works: Switching tasks is extra hard with ADHD and autism; a small, repeatable ritual tells your brain 'we're changing gears now'.

name: Permission to rest
steps: You're allowed to rest. {task} will be saved for later, right where you left it.
Rest however feels good. Coming back later is always an option.
literal_version: Stop working now. {task} is saved. You can return to it later.
Do something restful for at least 10 minutes.
phrasings: Your battery matters too. Want to rest instead?
Rest is part of the work. {task} can wait for you.
why_it_works: Pushing on an empty tank makes the next start harder; real rest refills the energy that starting needs.

name: Sensory reset
steps: Let's turn the input down: dim your screen, put on headphones or earplugs, and give yourself one quiet minute.
When it feels a bit softer, decide: look at {task}, or rest a little longer. Both are fine.
literal_version: Lower your screen brightness. Put on headphones or earplugs. Sit quietly for 1 minute.
After 1 minute, choose: open {task}, or rest for 5 more minutes.
phrasings: Things might be a bit loud right now. Want to turn the world down a notch?
A quiet minute first?
why_it_works: Sensory overload uses up the same energy that starting needs; lowering input gives your nervous system room to settle.

name: Name the first move
steps: What's the very first physical move for {task} — a click, a scroll, picking up a pen? Do only that move.
Next physical move. Just one.
literal_version: Decide the first physical action for {task} (for example: click the file, pick up a pen). Do only that action.
Do the next single physical action.
phrasings: Forget the whole thing. What would your hand do first?
Let's find the first move your body makes for {task}.
why_it_works: Big tasks feel abstract; a concrete physical action skips the planning loop and gets your body moving first.

name: Write the title
steps: Type just the title of {task} at the top of the page. Your name counts too.
Add today's date under it. Look at that — it's started.
literal_version: Type the title of {task} at the top of the document.
Type today's date below the title.
phrasings: Want to just put a title on {task}?
Tiniest writing step: a title for {task}.
why_it_works: A blank page is intimidating; a title makes the document 'already started', which takes the edge off.

name: Copy the question
steps: Copy the assignment question for {task} into your document, word for word. That's real progress.
Underline the one word in the question that matters most.
literal_version: Copy the question or instructions for {task}. Paste them at the top of your document.
Underline the most important word in the question.
phrasings: Let's borrow the first words from the question itself.
Copy-paste counts as starting {task}.
why_it_works: Copying is low-effort and puts the task in front of you, so you're working before your brain notices.

name: Three messy bullets
steps: Jot three messy bullet points of what {task} needs. Typos welcome.
Circle the smallest bullet. That's where we start.
literal_version: Write three bullet points listing what {task} needs.
Choose the shortest bullet point. Start with that one.
phrasings: Want to get {task} out of your head and onto the page?
Three bullets, zero pressure?
why_it_works: Working memory is limited; putting the parts on paper frees your brain to pick one instead of juggling all of them.

name: Explain it to me
steps: Tell me in one sentence what {task} is about, out loud or typed. I'm listening.
Now say what the first part of it would be.
literal_version: Say one sentence that explains what {task} is about.
Say what the first part of {task} is.
phrasings: Want to explain {task} to me like I'm a friend?
Talking it out can unlock it. What's {task} about?
why_it_works: Explaining out loud organizes your thoughts and often reveals the first step on its own.

name: One window, one thing
steps: Drag {task} into its own window so it's the only thing in front of you. Your other tabs are safe, just out of view.
Maximize that window and look at it for one minute.
literal_version: Drag the tab with {task} out into a new window. Your other tabs stay open in the old window.
Make the new window full size. Look at {task} for 1 minute.
phrasings: Want to give {task} a quiet room of its own?
Let's clear the stage so {task} is the only thing on it.
why_it_works: Fewer visible options means fewer pulls on attention, without the stress of closing anything.

name: Gentle 10-minute round
steps: Try a 10-minute round on {task} with body-double mode. You can press stop any time, no explanation needed.
Round done? Take a 2-minute stretch before deciding on another.
literal_version: Press 'Start body-double mode' below. A 10-minute timer starts. Work on {task}. You may stop at any time.
When the timer ends, stand up and stretch for 2 minutes.
phrasings: Feeling a little steadier? A short round on {task} might fit.
Ten calm minutes with {task}, exit door always open?
why_it_works: Short, bounded work rounds with a built-in exit feel safe to start, and the visible timer helps with time blindness.

name: Pair it with a treat
steps: Grab a drink or snack you enjoy, then open {task} while you have it.
Enjoy it while you do one small piece of {task}.
literal_version: Get a drink or snack you like. Then open {task}.
Do one small part of {task} while you eat or drink.
phrasings: What if {task} came with a snack?
Let's make {task} a bit more pleasant first.
why_it_works: Pairing a pleasant thing with a hard thing (temptation bundling) lends the hard thing a bit of reward.

name: Stand, stretch, sit
steps: Stand up, reach your arms up high once, then sit back down and open {task}.
Shake out your hands, then do the first small part.
literal_version: Stand up. Raise both arms above your head. Sit down. Open {task}.
Shake your hands for 5 seconds. Do the first small part of {task}.
phrasings: Want to wake your body up a little before {task}?
A quick stretch might shake loose a start.
why_it_works: A small burst of movement nudges alertness and gives your brain a clean 'reset' before starting.

name: Brain dump
steps: Let's empty your head first. Press Brain dump and ramble about everything on your mind. I'll pick one thing to start with.
Here's the one thing I'd start with. Want to swap it for another?
literal_version: Press 'Open brain dump' below. Say or type every task you are thinking about. Nudge will group them and choose one.
Look at the chosen task. Keep it or choose a different one.
phrasings: Too many things at once? Let's pour them all out.
Your head sounds full. Want to unload it here?
why_it_works: When everything feels urgent, nothing gets started; getting it all out lets you choose one thing with less noise.

name: Easiest part first
steps: Find the easiest part of {task}, even if it's not the first part. Start there.
Another easy bit? Keep picking the low-hanging fruit.
literal_version: Look at {task}. Choose the easiest part. Do that part first.
Choose the next easiest part and do it.
phrasings: Who says you have to start at the start?
Let's grab the easiest piece of {task}.
why_it_works: An early easy win builds momentum and proves to your brain that this task is doable.

name: Look at what you've done
steps: Take a peek at what you've already done today (tap 'Show today's wins'). Every start counts, including the ones that paused.
With that in mind, pick one tiny next thing, or rest. Your call.
literal_version: Press 'Show today's wins' below. Read what you did today.
Choose one small next action for {task}, or choose to rest.
phrasings: You've done more than it feels like. Want to see?
Quick look back before looking forward?
why_it_works: Seeing evidence of effort counters the 'I've done nothing' feeling that often makes restarting harder.

name: Note to future-you
steps: Write one line to future-you about where {task} is at and what the next tiny bit could be.
That's a gift to later-you. Rest or continue — both are fine.
literal_version: Write one sentence describing where {task} is now and what the next step is.
Choose: rest now, or continue {task}.
phrasings: Want to leave a breadcrumb for future-you?
Let's make tomorrow's start easier.
why_it_works: Restarting is easiest when you know exactly where to pick up; a one-line note saves future-you the 'where was I?' search.

name: Phone in another room
steps: Put your phone face-down across the room for just this one step. It'll be right there afterwards.
Now look at {task} for one minute.
literal_version: Place your phone face-down at least 2 metres away from you.
Look at {task} for 1 minute.
phrasings: Want to give your phone a short nap?
A little distance from the phone, just for now?
why_it_works: Even a silent phone nearby pulls on attention; a little distance removes one competing choice.

name: Read one paragraph
steps: Read just the first paragraph of {task}. Nothing else is needed.
Read the next paragraph, or stop and let it sink in.
literal_version: Read the first paragraph of {task}. Then stop.
Read the second paragraph of {task}, or stop.
phrasings: One paragraph, and that's it?
Let's just read a little of {task}.
why_it_works: A clearly defined, tiny reading goal has a visible finish line, which makes it easier to begin.

name: Highlight one line
steps: Find and highlight one sentence in {task} that looks important.
Highlight one more, or write a one-word note beside it.
literal_version: Highlight one sentence in {task} that seems important.
Highlight one more sentence, or write a one-word note next to it.
phrasings: Treasure hunt: one important line in {task}?
Want to just mark one sentence?
why_it_works: Highlighting is active but low-stakes, so it switches your brain into 'working' mode gently.

name: Empty headings
steps: Make empty headings for {task}, like Intro, Middle, End. No content yet.
Pick the heading that feels easiest and add one line under it.
literal_version: Type three headings in your document: 'Introduction', 'Main part', 'Conclusion'. Do not write anything under them.
Choose one heading. Write one sentence under it.
phrasings: Want to build the skeleton of {task} first?
Headings only, no pressure to fill them.
why_it_works: A scaffold turns one big task into small labelled boxes, which are far easier to start than a blank page.

name: Two questions
steps: Write down two questions you have about {task}. Questions count as real work.
Choose one question and look for its answer for two minutes.
literal_version: Write two questions about {task}.
Choose one question. Spend 2 minutes looking for the answer.
phrasings: What don't you know yet about {task}? That's a great start.
Confusion is useful. Want to write it down?
why_it_works: Unclear tasks are hard to start; naming what's unclear turns fog into something you can act on.

name: Peek at an example
steps: Find one example or solved problem similar to {task} and look at it for a minute.
Copy its shape: what's the first thing it does? Do that for yours.
literal_version: Find one solved example similar to {task}. Read it for 1 minute.
Look at the first step in the example. Do the same first step for {task}.
phrasings: Want to see how someone else started something like {task}?
Examples can be a map. Peek at one?
why_it_works: Examples reduce the uncertainty about 'how do I even begin', which is often what freezes a start.

name: Draft a question to someone
steps: Draft a one-line message to a friend, classmate, or TA with one question about {task}. Sending it is optional.
If it feels okay, send it. If not, the draft still helped you think.
literal_version: Write a one-sentence message asking one question about {task}. Do not send it yet.
Choose: send the message, or keep it as a note.
phrasings: Want to borrow a brain for {task}?
Sometimes one question to someone unlocks the whole thing.
why_it_works: Reaching out breaks isolation, and writing a question clarifies what you actually need.

name: Water first
steps: Get a glass of water. Then see how you feel about {task} — no decision needed yet.
Feeling a touch better? Open {task}, or rest more. Both are good choices.
literal_version: Go and drink a glass of water.
Choose: open {task}, or rest for 10 more minutes.
phrasings: When did you last have some water?
A water break first might help.
why_it_works: Even mild dehydration can make focus and mood harder; it's one of the easiest things to fix.

name: Body check-in
steps: Quick body check: hungry, thirsty, tired, too warm, too cold? Pick one and look after it first.
Now, how does {task} feel? Start tiny or rest — you choose.
literal_version: Ask yourself: Am I hungry, thirsty, tired, hot, or cold? Fix one of these.
Choose: start a small part of {task}, or rest.
phrasings: Sometimes 'stuck' is actually 'hungry'. Quick check?
How's your body doing right now?
why_it_works: Unmet body needs quietly drain executive function; meeting one often frees up more energy than pushing harder.

name: Pick your stopping point
steps: Before starting, pick your exit: "I'll stop after one paragraph" (or one problem). Then begin {task}.
Reached your stopping point? That's a full win. Stop or continue, your choice.
literal_version: Decide where you will stop, for example: after one paragraph or one question. Then start {task}.
When you reach that point, you may stop.
phrasings: Knowing where it ends can make starting easier.
Let's give {task} a finish line you choose.
why_it_works: Tasks with no clear end feel endless; a chosen stopping point makes starting feel safe.

name: Switch to paper
steps: Switch tools: grab paper or a whiteboard and sketch the first idea for {task} by hand.
Bring one line from the paper back into your document.
literal_version: Take a pen and paper. Write or draw your first idea for {task}.
Type one line from the paper into your document.
phrasings: Want to step away from the screen for a moment?
Paper sometimes feels less scary than a screen.
why_it_works: A different medium is a small novelty, and paper has no tabs pulling you away.

name: Say the first draft
steps: Say your first idea for {task} out loud, like you're telling a friend. Then type the gist of what you said.
Say the next idea out loud, then jot it down.
literal_version: Say your first idea about {task} out loud. Then type a short version of it.
Say your second idea out loud. Then type it.
phrasings: Talking is often easier than writing. Want to say it first?
What would you say about {task} if nobody was grading it?
why_it_works: Speaking skips the blank-page freeze; ideas that come out by voice are easier to tidy than to invent.

name: 5-4-3-2-1 launch
steps: Count down 5-4-3-2-1 and click into {task} on 1. No thinking in between.
You launched. Do one small thing while you're there.
literal_version: Count down from 5 to 1. When you say 1, click on {task}.
Do one small action in {task}.
phrasings: Want to launch into {task} like a little rocket?
Countdown start?
why_it_works: A countdown interrupts overthinking and gives a clear 'go' moment.

name: Tiny side win
steps: Do one tiny unrelated win: clear one corner of your desk or throw away one thing. Then come back to {task}.
Momentum's warm. Open {task}.
literal_version: Clean one small area of your desk. Keep it under 2 minutes.
Open {task}.
phrasings: A quick easy win might warm up your engine.
Want to start with something tiny and easy?
why_it_works: A small finished action gives a little reward and momentum you can carry into the bigger task.

name: Sound bubble
steps: Turn on brown noise or rain in body-double mode, then look at {task} inside your little sound bubble.
Stay in the bubble and do one small piece.
literal_version: Press 'Start body-double mode' below. Under 'Background sound', choose 'Brown noise (deep, soft)' or 'Rain-ish'. Open {task}.
Do one small part of {task} while the sound plays.
phrasings: Some steady background sound might help.
Want a cosy sound bubble for {task}?
why_it_works: Steady background noise can mask distracting sounds and give an under-stimulated brain just enough input.

name: Same start routine
steps: Do your usual start ritual — same drink, same playlist, same seat. Then open {task}.
Ritual done. One small step on {task}.
literal_version: Do the same three things you usually do before work (for example: get a drink, start a playlist, sit at your desk). Then open {task}.
Do one small part of {task}.
phrasings: Your usual start ritual might carry you in.
Familiar steps can make {task} feel familiar too.
why_it_works: Predictable routines reduce the number of decisions needed to begin, which helps both ADHD and autistic brains.

name: Grounding pressure
steps: Try something grounding: wrap up in a hoodie or blanket, or press your palms together firmly for a slow count of ten.
When you feel a bit more settled, choose: rest, or one tiny look at {task}.
literal_version: Press your palms together firmly and count slowly to 10. Or wrap yourself in a blanket.
Choose: rest, or look at {task} for 1 minute.
phrasings: Want to feel a little more grounded first?
Let's settle your body before anything else.
why_it_works: Deep pressure is calming for many autistic and ADHD nervous systems and can ease overwhelm quickly.

name: Write the exact order
steps: Write the exact order of the next three actions for {task}, so nothing is a surprise.
Do action number one.
literal_version: Write a numbered list of the next 3 actions for {task}. Be specific.
Do action 1 on your list.
phrasings: Would a clear, predictable order help with {task}?
Let's take the guesswork out of {task}.
why_it_works: Uncertainty is exhausting; a concrete order removes surprises and the decisions that come with them.

name: Aim for 1%
steps: Change the goal from "finish {task}" to "make it 1% more done". What's 1%?
Do that 1%. It genuinely counts.
literal_version: Choose one very small piece of {task} — about 1% of it.
Do that piece.
phrasings: What would 1% of {task} look like?
Let's shrink the goal until it's easy.
why_it_works: A smaller goal shrinks the fear that blocks starting; momentum does the rest more often than you'd expect.

name: First checkbox
steps: Open the instructions or rubric for {task} and turn the first point into a checkbox.
Look at that one checkbox. What's the tiniest move toward it?
literal_version: Open the instructions for {task}. Write the first requirement as a checkbox item.
Do one small action for that checkbox.
phrasings: Want to turn the instructions into a checklist?
Let's find the first box to tick.
why_it_works: Checklists externalize what's needed and give a satisfying sense of progress with each tick.

name: Short walk
steps: Take a short walk — even to the end of the corridor and back. Fresh air is a bonus.
Back? Notice how you feel, then choose rest or a tiny step.
literal_version: Walk for 5 minutes. You can walk to the end of the hallway and back.
When you return, choose: rest, or do one small part of {task}.
phrasings: Your brain might like a little walk.
A few minutes of moving could reset things.
why_it_works: Light movement can lift mood and alertness and gives your mind a break from the stuck loop.

name: Kind words first
steps: Put a hand on your chest and say: "This is hard, and I'm still allowed to try."
When you're ready, the smallest next thing is just to look at {task}.
literal_version: Place one hand on your chest. Say: 'This is hard. I am allowed to try.'
Look at {task} when you feel ready.
phrasings: This seems hard right now. That makes sense.
Before anything else: you're doing okay.
why_it_works: Self-criticism makes avoidance stronger; self-compassion lowers the threat so starting feels possible again.

name: Make it new
steps: Change one thing about how {task} looks: a new font, a different colour pen, dark mode, or standing up.
With the fresh look, do one small piece.
literal_version: Change one setting: the font, the colour, or switch to dark mode. Or stand while you work.
Do one small part of {task}.
phrasings: Want to give {task} a makeover?
A little novelty might wake things up.
why_it_works: ADHD attention responds to novelty; a fresh look can make a stale task feel new enough to begin.

name: Start from the end
steps: Start from the end: jot down what the finished {task} would say or show, in one line.
Now work backwards one step from there.
literal_version: Write one sentence describing what the finished {task} will contain.
Write the step that comes just before the finished version.
phrasings: What if we started from the finish line?
Let's peek at what done looks like.
why_it_works: Picturing the end clarifies the goal and makes the path backwards easier to see.

name: Pick up the thread
steps: Let's pick up right where you were. Reread just the last line you wrote or read in {task}.
Add one tiny thing after it.
literal_version: Go to the last place you worked on in {task}. Read the last sentence.
Add one sentence or one small action after it.
phrasings: No need to start over. Let's find your place.
Your progress is still there. Want to peek?
why_it_works: Rereading the last bit reloads your context so continuing feels like a small step, not a fresh start.

name: Make time visible
steps: Start the visual timer below so you can see time moving, then glance at {task} while it runs.
Watch the ring shrink while you do one small thing.
literal_version: Press 'Start the visual timer' below. Look at {task} while it runs.
Do one small action in {task} before the timer ends.
phrasings: Time can feel slippery. Want to see it?
A visible timer might make {task} feel more contained.
why_it_works: Time blindness makes tasks feel endless; seeing time pass makes the effort feel bounded and real.

name: Choose between two
steps: Here are two tiny options: open {task}, or write one word about it. Pick either — both count.
You chose. Do just that one.
literal_version: Choose one: (A) open {task}, or (B) write one word about {task}.
Do the option you chose.
phrasings: Too many choices? Here are just two.
Let's make this an easy pick.
why_it_works: Fewer options reduce decision fatigue, and choosing gives a sense of control.

name: Call it a day kindly
steps: It might be time to call it a day. I'll save {task} for later with a note so starting again is easy.
Rest well. Nothing is lost.
literal_version: Stop for today. Nudge will save {task} and a note for next time.
Close your laptop when you are ready.
phrasings: You've given what you had today. That's enough.
Want to close up for today? It's a perfectly good choice.
why_it_works: Ending on purpose (instead of drifting) protects tomorrow's energy and makes the next start easier.

name: One quiet minute
steps: Close your eyes or soften your gaze for one minute. Nothing to do, nothing to fix.
How do you feel? Rest a bit more or try something tiny — both are fine.
literal_version: Close your eyes for 1 minute. Breathe normally.
Choose: rest more, or do one small part of {task}.
phrasings: Want one minute where nothing is asked of you?
A tiny pause might help everything feel smaller.
why_it_works: A short pause lets a stressed nervous system downshift so the task feels less threatening.

name: Count the parts
steps: Just count how many parts or questions {task} has. Counting is the whole step.
Pick the shortest part from your count.
literal_version: Count the number of questions or sections in {task}. Write the number down.
Choose the shortest question or section.
phrasings: How big is {task} really? Let's count.
Sometimes knowing the size makes it smaller.
why_it_works: Unknown size feels infinite; counting gives the task a real, finite shape.

name: Set up the space
steps: Set up your space for {task}: open the right file, put your notes beside you. Don't start yet.
Everything's ready. Want to do one tiny thing now that it's set up?
literal_version: Open the files you need for {task}. Put your notes on the desk. Do not start working yet.
Choose: do one small action, or stop here.
phrasings: What if you just got things ready for {task}?
Setting up counts as starting.
why_it_works: Preparing removes friction for later, and it often slides naturally into starting.

name: Busy hands
steps: Grab something for your hands — a fidget, a pen to click, a hair tie — then look at {task}.
Keep fidgeting while you do one small piece.
literal_version: Hold a small object you can fidget with. Then open {task}.
Do one small part of {task} while holding the object.
phrasings: Restless? Let your hands have something to do.
A fidget might help {task} feel easier.
why_it_works: Small movements can give a restless ADHD brain the stimulation it seeks, freeing attention for the task.
